title: Live Institutional Risk Engine
description: A live risk-monitoring engine: any listed company or benchmark in, market risk recalculated on demand, through an interactive dashboard. All 14 phases are built: tiered data validation, volatility, beta, drawdown, Value at Risk by three independent methods, Expected Shortfall, GARCH(1,1) conditional volatility, formal VaR backtesting, portfolio risk, and fundamental and valuation risk that reuse the other two engines rather than reimplementing them. The final phase combines all three into one composite view that names where they disagree, which turned out to be the actual point of building it.
highlights: Every fetch is timestamped and classified DELAYED or STALE by measured age, never LIVE, because yfinance carries no real-time service guarantee. "Live" in this engine means refreshable on demand and recalculated from current data, not real-time, and the code states that distinction rather than quietly claiming more than the data source supports.

Value at Risk is built three independent ways so the assumptions can be compared rather than trusted. The interesting result is that the normal model's error changes sign with the confidence level: at 95% it is more conservative than the empirical figure (S&P 1.81% against 1.66%), at 99% it understates by 28%. Fitting a normal to a fat-tailed sample inflates sigma to absorb the extreme days, pushing the moderate quantiles too far out while still falling short in the far tail, so a normal VaR cannot be called conservative or optimistic without saying where it is being read.

Expected Shortfall exposes a failure VaR hides. The normal assumption is 22% below the empirical figure on VaR but 38% below on Expected Shortfall, because a normal has a fixed thin tail and its ES/VaR ratio is pinned near 1.15 regardless of the data while the real ratio is 1.45. The Student-t turns out to model the tail's shape better than its threshold, understating VaR while getting ES nearly right.

VaR's incoherence is demonstrated in code rather than cited: two independent positions each with a 95% VaR of -0.02 combine into a portfolio VaR of 0.49, so VaR claims diversification created risk. That demonstration then caught a real bug in the engine's own Expected Shortfall code, because it reported ES as non-subadditive, which is mathematically impossible and so could only be an implementation error: the tail had been selected as "values below the quantile", which on a distribution with an atom selects the entire sample and silently turns a 5% ES into the mean of everything.

GARCH(1,1) makes the estimate conditional, which is the difference between "how bad is a bad day for this asset in general" and "how bad is a bad day this week". The model is justified before it is fitted rather than after: an ARCH-LM test runs first, and on the S&P it returns p = 2.3e-167 before fitting and p = 0.314 on the standardised residuals afterwards, which is the pair worth reporting together.

Backtesting was built out of order, immediately after GARCH, because without it "GARCH is the better model" is an appeal to authority rather than a measurement. The verdict is a qualified yes, reported rather than tuned away: across the S&P, Apple and the Nifty 50, GARCH fixes breach clustering on every series (S&P 0.0030 to 0.4373), but on the Nifty it over-breaches badly enough to fail coverage outright, making it the worse of the two models there. The likely cause is a symmetric model applied to a market whose downside shocks are not symmetric, so those figures are documented as the weakest in the engine rather than presented alongside the rest.

Phases 9 and 10 are where the three engines meet, and neither recomputes anything: fundamental risk reads Module 1's ratios and valuation risk shocks Module 2's DCF, so there is one implementation of each calculation and no second copy free to drift. Both are optional dependencies, because the market-risk core stands on its own and someone who wants Value at Risk should not be made to install two other engines to get it.

Fundamental risk asks how fragile the business is, as opposed to how much the price moves, and names the divergence when the two disagree. Tesla scores 25 on fundamentals against 100 on market risk, where price volatility overstates business fragility. Pfizer is the reverse and the more dangerous direction: 52 against 26, with interest cover falling 7.4x per year and margins compressing 4.4 points per year, while the share price stays calm. A calm price is not evidence about the balance sheet, and volatility-based measures cannot see leverage building underneath a quiet stock.

The question is deliberately different from the health score in Module 1. Health is mostly profitability, and a highly profitable company can still be fragile, so here profitability barely features, earnings quality gets its own pillar, and direction outweighs level: a company at 2.5x interest cover that was 8x three years ago is more dangerous than one that has sat at 2.5x throughout, and a latest-year score cannot tell them apart.

Valuation risk measures sensitivity rather than level, since a valuation can sit exactly on the market price and still be worthless if a quarter point of discount rate moves it by half. The reverse stress test is the part worth having: instead of asking what a company is worth, it asks what today's price requires. For Apple that is terminal growth of 7.62% in perpetuity at the model's own cost of capital, far above nominal GDP growth and therefore something no business has ever sustained, which is a far sharper statement than "the model reads low".

Portfolio risk starts from the fact that variance is a quadratic form, not a weighted average. On an equally weighted portfolio of Apple, Microsoft, Johnson & Johnson, Exxon and Coca-Cola, every weight is 20% and no risk share is: Apple carries 30.0% of the portfolio's risk and Johnson & Johnson 11.0%, nearly three times apart for the same money. Risk contributions sum to portfolio volatility by Euler's theorem, asserted at runtime so a wrong decomposition fails rather than returning a plausible number, and a holding that moves against the book shows negative contribution because it reduces total volatility rather than adding to it.

Diversification is measured on both axes rather than asserted. That portfolio's weighted average volatility is 23.4% against an actual 14.2%, and its 99% VaR is 2.37% against 4.07% for the weighted sum of the holdings' own VaRs, because they do not all have their bad days together. Only the minimum-variance point on the efficient frontier is offered, since every other point needs return forecasts that carry far more estimation error than covariances and would dominate the answer.

A pathology found and suppressed rather than displayed: the GARCH model-implied long-run volatility came out at 48.6% annualised for the S&P against a realised 18.1%. The figure follows correctly from the fitted parameters and is meaningless, because it divides by one minus persistence, which is 0.002 here, and moving persistence from 0.995 to 0.999 swings the answer from 31% to 69%. It is now flagged unreliable and realised volatility is used as the benchmark instead, a measurement rather than an extrapolation.

248 tests across the thirteen phases built, split by a marker so the market-risk suite still runs without the other two engines installed. Several were cases where the test was right and the code was wrong: the reverse-stress solver gave up whenever the top of its search range was unsolvable, which is the cell most likely to fail since it sits closest to where the perpetuity formula breaks down.

The final phase (14) combines market, fundamental and valuation risk onto one scale rather than stopping at three separate readings, and the composite score turned out to be the least interesting thing it produces: the useful output is naming where the three disagree. Verified against the exact cases the earlier phases had already characterised, independently and without retuning anything for the demo. Apple shows genuine three-way agreement and correctly raises no divergence. Pfizer fires the dangerous one, fundamental risk (52) exceeding market risk (26) while 71% of its valuation sits in a terminal value assuming trend continuation against a deterioration score of 67, reproducing the same post-pandemic finding Phase 9 reached entirely on its own. Tesla shows the opposite pattern, extreme market risk (96) over modest fundamentals (25), the safer direction to be wrong in. A dimension that cannot be computed, such as an index with no filings, is dropped and the remaining weights renormalised rather than scored as safe, the same rule Module 1's health score applies to a missing metric.

title: Portfolio Construction & Investment Management Engine
description: Multi-asset portfolio construction, optimisation, risk and simulation platform on one assumption tree. The first module in this platform to depend on another module's package at the code level: it reuses the Live Institutional Risk Engine's own portfolio volatility, risk contribution, VaR and Expected Shortfall machinery rather than reimplementing it, and adds four constrained optimisation methods, a real efficient frontier, Monte Carlo simulation, stress testing and rebalancing on top.
highlights: Reuses risk_engine.portfolio and risk_engine.var_*/expected_shortfall — the already-built, already-tested Live Institutional Risk Engine — for portfolio volatility, Euler risk contribution, diversification ratio, Sharpe, drawdown and Herfindahl concentration, installed straight from that repository as a dependency rather than re-derived a second time.

All four optimisation methods (equal weight, minimum variance, maximum Sharpe, target return) route through scipy's constrained SLSQP solver rather than a closed-form matrix inversion, because a closed form cannot express the weight bounds, asset-class caps and long-only constraints this engine actually exposes as user inputs. The efficient frontier is 25 independently solved optimisations, not a smoothed curve between two points.

Found and fixed a real scipy bug: minimize()'s own args tuple is forwarded only to the objective function, never to functions in the constraints list. The target-return constraint originally expected extra positional arguments scipy never supplies; the fix closes over the needed values with default parameters instead, now the documented pattern for every constraint in the module.

Monte Carlo simulation offers both a bootstrap draw, which resamples whole historical days jointly across assets and, as a structural consequence, can never simulate a day worse than history's actual worst — verified directly by a dedicated test — and a parametric draw from the covariance matrix, which can exceed history's worst day but inherits the normal distribution's own understatement of extreme moves. Neither is presented as more correct than the other.

A user-supplied correlation matrix is checked for positive semi-definiteness before use: mutually inconsistent pairwise correlations (two pairs near +1 while the third is near -1) imply negative portfolio variance, a contradiction rather than a modelling choice, and are refused rather than silently accepted. Absent any correlation input, the engine defaults to independence and discloses that as a stated assumption rather than fabricating a plausible market-typical number.

Portfolio weights that don't sum to 100% are refused rather than silently renormalised, because renormalising would quietly change the portfolio the user thinks they specified — the same refuse-don't-guess discipline as every assumption in this platform.
Rebalancing costs are charged on the gross value traded, not netted: a buy in one asset offsetting a sell in another on paper still means two real trades, and both incur cost.

Verified live against five years of real daily prices for Apple, Microsoft, a 20+ Year Treasury ETF and Gold: 14.5% volatility, a 1.56 diversification ratio, a 99% historical VaR of 2.23% against a 2.69% Expected Shortfall (1.21x), and a largest risk contributor (AAPL, 37.8% of risk) that differs from the largest position by weight (25.0%) — the same weight-versus-risk finding the risk engine exists to surface. All twelve tabs (Dashboard through Audit) run with no exception against this data.

86 tests across the assumption engine, data layer, risk, optimization, simulation, stress, rebalancing, benchmark comparison and validation, including five test-construction bugs caught and fixed on the first full run — each one verified against the underlying calculation before the assertion was changed, not the other way around.

title: PE Valuation & Deal Analysis Engine
description: A private equity deal model that values one company two ways at once: a DCF for what the business is worth to a permanent owner, and a full LBO for what a sponsor can pay and still hit a target return. Every material assumption is a user input feeding one immutable assumption tree, so changing a growth rate moves the forecast, both valuations, the debt schedule, the sensitivity grids, the scenarios and the investment committee conclusion together. Nothing is hard-coded.
highlights: The DCF and the LBO answer different questions, and treating them as competing estimates of one number is the most common way the comparison is misread. The DCF values the business on its own cash flows with no view on who buys it. The LBO is a statement about the buyer's economics: leverage, a finite holding period and an exit. The gap between them is the deliverable rather than a tie-break.

The two models are provably independent, which is the clearest evidence they are correctly separated. Raising beta from 1.15 to 1.60 moves DCF enterprise value from 2,253 to 1,728 and leaves the IRR at exactly 20.3%, because the LBO never uses a discount rate: its return is solved, not assumed. Raising leverage from 5.0x to 6.5x lifts the IRR from 20.3% to 25.5% and leaves the DCF untouched, because unlevered free cash flow is independent of capital structure by construction. If either orthogonality broke, one model would be contaminating the other.

One immutable assumption tree feeds everything, so a DCF and an LBO cannot disagree because they were handed different growth rates. Immutability is not stylistic: a sensitivity grid runs eighty variants and the scenario engine runs three, and the single most common way a financial model produces a wrong number is state left behind from the previous run. A scenario is a new object, never a mutated global.

The interest circularity in an LBO is real and is resolved rather than avoided. Interest depends on the debt balance, which depends on how much cash is swept to repay it, which depends on interest. A beginning-balance convention breaks the loop; an average-balance convention does not, and the schedule is recomputed until the charge stops moving. Spreadsheets solve this by enabling iterative calculation and hoping; this engine iterates explicitly, caps the passes and reports whether it converged.

The value creation bridge has four components, not the usual three. EBITDA growth, multiple change and debt paydown do not sum to total value created: the missing term is the interaction between growth and multiple, the extra value from selling more EBITDA at a higher price, which belongs to neither lever alone. Many published bridges drop it and silently absorb the gap into EBITDA growth, flattering the operational story. Here the four sum exactly, the identity is asserted at runtime, and a test demonstrates that removing the fourth breaks it by precisely its own size.

The maximum entry price solver runs the model backwards, asking what a sponsor can pay to hit a target IRR rather than what return a price produces. Building it surfaced a real bug: below roughly 4.5x entry the debt raised exceeds the total funding requirement, so sponsor equity goes negative and IRR is undefined. Reading that as "target unreachable" reported the exact opposite of the truth, rejecting deals that work at a sensible price because they break at an absurd one. The solver now establishes the feasible range before bisecting.

Tax is handled differently in each model on purpose, and that is the substantive difference between them rather than an inconsistency. The DCF charges tax on unlevered EBIT and interest never enters the cash flow, because WACC already carries the debt shield in the discount rate; counting it twice is the most common way a DCF flatters itself. The LBO charges cash tax on profit after interest, because the sponsor genuinely deducts it and that shield is a real source of buyout returns.

Model validation is tiered rather than pass/fail, because a model that blocks on everything is unusable and one that blocks on nothing is untrustworthy. Terminal growth at or above WACC blocks outright, since the Gordon formula divides by their difference and the output would be an artefact of the division. Leverage above seven turns warns but proceeds. An exit multiple above the entry multiple is noted, since assuming multiple expansion is a bet on the market rather than on the business.

Every headline number has a Show calculation panel reconstructing it line by line, so it can be checked by hand rather than believed, and an audit trail maps each input to what it flows through and what it finally affects. The interface layer holds no financial calculations at all: it collects inputs, calls the engine and renders results, so all 75 tests sit on the part that matters.

title: AI Financial Analyst
description: An AI analyst that sits on top of the other three engines rather than beside them. The LLM decides what analysis a question needs and calls deterministic Python tools to get it; it never calculates a financial figure itself. Phase 1 of 16 is built: Modules 1, 2 and 3 are integrated behind one tool interface of 16 tools, each result tagged with whether it is a filed fact, a model calculation or a model assumption. The agent, RAG and dashboard are still to come.
highlights: The differentiator is what the LLM is not allowed to do. It selects tools and interprets results; every ratio, DCF, WACC, VaR and GARCH figure is computed by the existing Python engines and handed back. That makes the numbers reproducible and auditable rather than generated, which is the difference between a financial analyst and a chatbot with a finance vocabulary.

Integration was blocked by something no adapter code could fix: all three engines shipped a top-level package literally named "src", so Python resolves whichever appears first on the path and the other two become unreachable. The easy way out was vendoring copies into the new repo, which is how the analyst quietly becomes a fourth, divergent implementation of the same finance. Each engine was renamed to its own namespace and given packaging metadata instead, and the analyst now pins them as git dependencies, so a fix in an engine reaches it without anything being copied.

Two supporting problems surfaced during that work and were fixed rather than worked around. The risk engine reached into a sibling config directory through a sys.path insert, which works from a checkout and breaks the moment the package is installed. The valuation engine's entire pipeline lived inside its Streamlit app behind a cache decorator, so importing it ran page setup and tied a library's caching policy to the lifetime of a browser tab; the calculation moved into the package and the app now imports it and applies its own caching.

Provenance is enforced in code, not requested in a prompt. Every value is tagged where it is produced as a source fact, a model calculation or a model assumption, and a tool that tries to emit an AI interpretation or judgement raises an error. Those two labels belong to the agent layer, so a model-authored sentence cannot reach a reader wearing the same label as a figure taken from a filing.

Tools never raise at the model. Every call returns a result object, and a failure is a result carrying a readable reason rather than an exception. An exception gives a model nothing true to say and invites it to fill the silence, which is exactly the hallucination the architecture exists to prevent; an invented tool name gets back the list of real ones instead of a crash.

Each engine's own caveats travel with its numbers, because the model will never read a README. The valuation always carries the finding that its DCF reads below market and must not be quoted alone. Value at Risk returns all three methods together, since they disagree in a structured way and handing over one number invites it to be reported as the risk. Unconditional figures say they are unconditional, and market data is classified delayed or stale, never live.

22 tests split by a live marker: 16 offline tests pin the provenance rules and the never-raise guarantee, and 6 live tests are deliberately not mocked, because a tool layer tested only against mocks proves the mocks work. The live set imports all three engines in one process, runs real valuations and VaR, and checks the same tool works for more than one company.

title: Institutional-Style Valuation Engine
description: Valuation engine for Nifty (NSE) companies in INR, plus a Quick DCF mode for any listed company worldwide. Stages 1 to 7 run end to end: historical assumptions, forecast, FCFF, WACC, a discounted cash flow, comparable-company valuation, bull/base/bear scenarios with sensitivity tables, and Monte Carlo with a blended cross-method summary. A real error in the cost of capital was found and fixed along the way; the gap that remained afterward is reported rather than tuned away.
highlights: The DCF read below market on every one of 32 companies, a median of -74.7%. The first diagnosis published for it was wrong, and finding that out is the useful part: the story was that a GDP-capped terminal growth rate was starving the terminal value, which fitted the handful of examples that suggested it. Testing it across the whole universe killed it. The companies pinned at the highest growth the model allows read worst, not best (UltraTech -97.6%, Titan -92.7%), and raising every company to the ceiling moved the median only 8 points while the standard competitive-equilibrium fix made it worse.

The real error was in the cost of capital: India's country risk was being charged twice. The cost of equity used the rupee 10-year government yield plus a 7.5% total equity risk premium, but that premium is a mature-market premium plus an India country premium, and a total premium of that construction belongs on a default-free rate. The rupee 10-year is not one, and the 269bp it yields over the US 10-year is precisely the market's price of the inflation differential and sovereign risk the country premium then charges for again. Stripping the default spread before CAPM moved median WACC from 13.34% to 11.17% and closed 15 points of the gap.

The previous defence of that 7.5% premium is why the error survived as long as it did. It checked the rupee build against a dollar build (Treasury + mature premium + country premium, inflation-adjusted), got 14.5% both ways, and concluded the number was sound. Both routes added the country premium, so agreeing with each other confirmed only that the same mistake had been made twice. A check that cannot fail is not a check. The two routes now agree within 70bp rather than disagreeing by 250bp.

The remaining gap is reported, not closed. A -59.9% median is still a long way from fair value, and it concentrates in two groups: capital-intensive companies earning less on capital than their cost of capital, where the reinvestment identity charges UltraTech 88% of NOPAT to fund GDP-rate growth and a DCF is arguably the wrong instrument for a cyclical; and richly-rated consumer franchises, where the original terminal-value intuition may still be part of the answer even though it failed as a universe-wide explanation. Nothing was tuned to make the numbers agree.

Comparable-company valuation is what made any of this diagnosable. It prices a company off what the market pays for its sector peers rather than off its own forecast, so it shares almost none of the DCF's machinery and carries no discount rate at all, which makes it a fixed benchmark across the whole investigation: +2.9% median throughout, against the DCF's -74.7% before and -59.9% after. Two methods built on the same statements moving apart rather than together is what ruled out a data bug from the start. For TCS the two now agree within 7% of the current price, where before they were 17 points apart.

Stage 7's Monte Carlo takes every distribution width from something measured rather than chosen, because a Monte Carlo with invented variances is the modeller's guess with error bars drawn on it and looks far more authoritative than the guess did alone. Growth and margin dispersion come from the company's own history; the discount rate's uncertainty is propagated from the regression standard error of beta, so a poorly estimated beta produces a genuinely wider valuation; and terminal growth, the one driver describing a period that has not happened, gets a bounded uniform rather than an invented mean and variance.

Growth and margin are drawn correlated, because operating leverage ties them together in a downturn and drawing them independently would let good growth pair with bad margin as often as bad with bad, cancelling much of the tail. Narrowness produced by a modelling shortcut is indistinguishable from precision, which is the specific way this kind of model misleads. Failed trials, where drawn terminal growth exceeds drawn WACC and the perpetuity has no finite value, are counted rather than dropped: discarding them would remove exactly the bad draws and bias the reported distribution upward.

The headline output is a probability, not a number: the share of trials valuing the company above its current price. Percentiles rather than the mean are reported, because the Gordon-growth denominator produces a long right tail as drawn terminal growth approaches drawn WACC, and the mean sits where no trial clusters.

The final summary reports a range and refuses to average the DCF and comparables when they span more than 40% of the current price. A DCF at -60% and comparables at +3% have a midpoint near -30%, and no analysis supports -30%; the disagreement is the result. Monte Carlo's median is carried as context rather than as a third method, since it is the same DCF sampled over its own inputs and would double-count that view against the one genuinely independent method.

Quick DCF mode values any listed company worldwide from a typed name, fetched live, with the currency-resolution logic that handles London quotes in pence, companies reporting in one currency and trading in another, and currency flags that are simply wrong. It deliberately offers no comparables, because real sector peers do not exist for an arbitrary company the way they do for the curated 33, and an auto-discovered peer group would quietly break the one property that made the calibration work possible.

Earlier fixes kept in the record: terminal reinvestment made consistent with terminal growth across the whole forecast rather than only the final year (which moved Reliance from an unusable 22 rupees a share to 323), FCFF built unlevered so the debt tax shield is not counted twice against WACC, working capital anchored on the recent level rather than a ten-year median that described no state the business was ever in, and negative equity value floored at zero for display since no equity trades below zero under limited liability.

100 tests across the seven stages, covering the reinvestment identity, currency resolution in both directions, multiple exclusion on negative denominators, scenario independence, sensitivity-grid monotonicity, the negative-equity floor, the Cholesky correlation surviving the draw, and the blended summary refusing to average methods that disagree.

title: Financial Statement Intelligence Engine
description: Type a company name, get its financial health, in any market: US, Europe, India, Japan. US listings use 10 years of SEC EDGAR filings; everywhere else uses Yahoo Finance. Also runs as a 20-company batch producing a 23-page report.
highlights: Works for any listed company, not a fixed list. A Streamlit app takes a name or ticker, resolves it (including cross-listings, which it shows rather than silently picking one), and scores it live. Verified across five markets: Apple through EDGAR at 10 years, ASML, Shell, Nestle and Reliance through Yahoo Finance.

Currency is where a global loader silently produces a plausible wrong answer instead of an error, and three traps are handled: London quotes in pence, not pounds (Shell's "3320.0" GBp read as GBP overstates the price 100x); the reporting currency is not always the quote currency (Infosys reports in USD, trades in INR); and the currency flag itself lies in both directions (HCL Technologies is tagged USD while reporting in rupees). The check is market capitalisation, which is unambiguously in the quote currency — except between currencies of similar size (USD vs GBP at 0.79), where that test can't discriminate and the source's own tag is used instead.
Foreign issuers file 20-F, not 10-K, so EDGAR returns nothing for Shell or SAP despite both being US-listed. The loader falls back to Yahoo Finance automatically rather than failing.

Every figure comes from filed 10-K data via the SEC EDGAR XBRL API for US companies, across 20 companies and 10 fiscal years in the batch report. Nothing is hand-entered, and the spot checks tie out to the filings (NVIDIA FY2025 revenue $130.5B, Microsoft FY2025 $281.7B, Tesla 2024 $97.69B).

Most of the engineering went into making EDGAR usable. Companies migrate between GAAP tags mid-history after ASC 606, so values are merged across an ordered list of candidate tags rather than taken from the first tag that returns anything, which took NVIDIA and Tesla from 6 usable years to 10.

Oil majors and several pharma companies never tag an operating income line, so EBIT is rebuilt from pretax income plus interest expense. Without that fallback, Exxon, Chevron, J&J, Merck and Pfizer produced no usable years at all.

EPS growth is deliberately excluded from the score. A 10-K restates only the roughly three years it covers, so Apple's FY2018 EPS reads 11.91 in one filing and 2.98 in another after the 4-for-1 split. Growth is scored on revenue and net income, which splits cannot distort.

The score refuses to invent results where data is missing: unavailable metrics are dropped, the remaining weights in that pillar are renormalized, and the exclusions are disclosed on each company's page. This caught negative book equity at Home Depot and AbbVie, where a negative debt-to-equity had been clamping to a perfect leverage score and overstating AbbVie by four points.

The resulting ranking is the clearest evidence of the method's own weakness, which is the point. The top four are all asset-light software and advertising businesses while Walmart lands 18th, because absolute thresholds measure the business model more than how well the company is run. Peer-relative scoring is the next module.

Full threshold table, fiscal-year convention and known limitations are published in the report and README, so any score can be recalculated or argued with. Backed by 26 tests covering the negative-equity, zero-interest, weight-renormalization and currency-resolution edge cases.

title: Investment Committee Dashboard
description: A six-page decision terminal that turns financial analysis, valuation, risk and AI research into one BUY/HOLD/SELL memo, stating the explicit thresholds that would change the call.
highlights: Six pages, not one screen: overview, financial analysis, valuation, risk, AI research and an investment-committee memo, each built for a different reviewer's question.
The memo states the recommendation alongside the specific financial thresholds that would flip it, rather than a static, one-time conclusion.
Every chart on the valuation and risk pages links back to the same underlying model output the AI analyst cites, so the dashboard and the AI never disagree.
Designed to answer whether the company is healthy, what it's worth, and what could go wrong within a few minutes for someone seeing it for the first time.
